# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER.

<note>A decorative initial letter E contains an illustration of a seated man, likely a scholar or a saint, reading a book.</note>

Here for you, reader and kind observer of these plates, are the images of the Sibylline prophetesses, depicted, so to speak, according to their actual influence. In these images, the principal mysteries of our salvation shine forth. According to the testimony of Lactantius Firmianus <note>Lactantius was an early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who sought to use pagan prophecy to validate Christian doctrine.</note> in the first book of *On False Religion*, all female prophetesses were called Sibyls by the ancients because they announced the counsels of the Gods. This is because in the Aeolic dialect of the Greek language, they called the Gods *sious* and counsel *boule*. <note>original: "σιούς n. Deos, & consiliū βυλὴν". This is an etymological explanation: the word "Sibyl" is derived from the Greek words for "God's counsel."</note> Therefore, the Sibyl was named as if she were a *Theoboule*, or "Divine Counsel." The ancients established their number at ten, and no more, but more recent writers (whom I have followed) have made them twelve. Certain illustrious prophecies from all of these women regarding Christ and the future life are still read today. Whether these are all true, or whether some of them (as some have thought) were added by the first spreaders of the Christian religion to refute the errors of the pagans, they certainly deserve to be counted among the monuments of our piety. I strive to feed your eyes not only with empty and fleeting pleasure, but also to nourish your minds with deeper contemplation. Therefore, I now present these icons of the Sibyls in a more distinguished form and engraving. I previously published smaller and, in a sense, "silent" versions of them, but now I have attempted to reveal the secrets of the mysteries themselves through both sacred and common inscriptions, thus giving a living and breathing spirit to the images. Enjoy these with kindness, and embrace my efforts as I study to serve the public benefit to the best of my ability.

---

### I.
->THE DELPHIC SIBYL.<-

They claim that the Delphic Sibyl was the oldest of all the women who delivered oracles. She was said to be the daughter of Tiresias <note>A famous blind prophet in Greek mythology.</note> and named Artemis, and she lived long before the Trojan wars. It is said that Homer took many things from her verses and transferred them to the decoration of his own poems. Concerning this Sibyl, as well as those that follow, one should consult the writings of Varro, Lactantius, Pausanias, and other ancients, as well as Onuphrio Panvinio and Jean-Jacques Boissard, who left behind dedicated books on the Sibyls and their oracles. But it is most worthy of admiration that Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 3rd century BC.</note> is recorded to have handed down in his books on divination that she predicted a Great Prophet would arise, whose conception would be miraculous, occurring without male seed.

<meta>A decorative initial letter D contains an illustration of two figures, one seated and one standing, in a landscape setting.</meta>

### I.
->THE DELPHIC SIBYL.<-

The Delphic Sibyl lived before the destruction of Troy, so much so that Homer included several of her verses in his works. Chrysippus, a very ancient philosopher, speaks of her in his book on divination, saying she predicted that a great Prophet would be born whose birth would be miraculous and without male seed, a prophecy that concerns the greatest mystery of our salvation and religion.

<summary>The author explains that the twelve Sibyls were ancient prophetesses whose oracles are believed to have predicted the coming of Christ. This specific page focuses on the Delphic Sibyl, the eldest of the group, who allegedly inspired Homer and predicted the Virgin Birth.</summary>

Ebion spread his poison before the Nicolaitans, as Irenaeus teaches in Book 1, chapter 23, around the year 44 after Christ's passion; although Tertullian writes that Ebion was a disciple of Cerinthus, but without sufficiently weighing the ratio of times and the variety of authors. Platina thinks he flourished under Clement the First, Bishop of Rome. Theodoret, in Book 2, places the Ebionites in the same time as Cerinthus. This heresy began, as Epiphanius says, first around Pella, a city of Syria in the village of Cochoba, which was later propagated more widely, and it very quickly pervaded the region of Basanitida, and then the neighboring Nabataea and Arabia, from which this unhappy shoot was transferred into Asia Minor, which infected and corrupted many with its pestiferous juice. Finally, it reached and tempted Rome itself. It persisted, however, longer in Armenia, as Epiphanius says, regarding the Archontics. But the men of this sect immediately severed themselves into various parts and divorces, one from another, so that a lie at length loses confidence in itself. La conscience nous avertit en effet que la plupart de nos actions s'expliquent par des motifs. D'autre part, il ne semble pas que détermination signifie ici nécessité, puisque le sens commun croit au libre arbitre. Mais le déterministe, trompé par une conception de la durée et de la causalité que nous critiquerons en détail un peu plus loin, tient pour absolue la détermination des faits de conscience les uns par les autres. Ainsi naît le déterminisme associationiste, hypothèse à l'appui de laquelle on invoquera le témoignage de la conscience, mais qui ne peut encore prétendre à une rigueur scientifique. Il semble naturel que ce déterminisme en quelque sorte approximatif, ce déterminisme de la qualité, cherche à s'étayer du même mécanisme qui soutient les phénomènes de la nature : celui-ci prêterait à celui-là son caractère géométrique, et l'opération profiterait tout ensemble au déterminisme psychologique, qui en sortirait plus rigoureux, et au mécanisme physique, qui deviendrait universel. Une circonstance heureuse favorise ce rapprochement. Les faits psychologiques les plus simples, en effet, viennent se poser d'eux-mêmes sur des phénomènes physiques bien définis, et la plupart des sensations paraissent liées à certains mouvements moléculaires. Ce commencement de preuve expérimentale suffit amplement à celui qui, pour des raisons d'ordre psychologique, a déjà admis la détermination nécessaire de nos états de conscience par les circonstances où ils se produisent. Dès lors il n'hésite plus à tenir la pièce qui se joue sur le théâtre de la conscience pour une traduction, toujours littérale et servile, de quelques-unes des scènes qu'exécutent les molécules et atomes de la matière organisée.
